title: Appendix: Cloud Patterns and Practices
overview: Use this appendix to choose patterns by the problem they solve. It connects container helpers, event sourcing, circuit breakers, CQRS, sagas, sharding, tenancy, aggregation and workflow coordination. For each pattern, identify its boundary and failure behaviour as well as its benefits.
big_ideas: A pattern is a reusable, named solution to a recurring problem in a context; cloud patterns evolved from VM to containers to cloud native.
Event sourcing records authoritative state changes as events; the append can be atomic while asynchronously updated read models lag.
CQRS splits write (command) and read (query) models; a read-only view DB is kept up to date by subscribing to domain events.
Saga keeps data consistent across services with local transactions plus compensating transactions, coordinated by choreography (events) or orchestration (a central orchestrator).
Circuit breaker fails fast when a downstream service's error rate passes a threshold, stopping cascading failure and thread exhaustion.
Sharding splits data by lookup, range or hash strategy to beat single-server limits on storage, compute, bandwidth and geography.
Multi-tenancy is a continuum: isolating gives customization, security and control; sharing gives economy of scale and simpler management (separate DB vs separate schema vs shared schema).
Content can be aggregated at the client, the API gateway, a composite microservice, or the database (ODS), each trading latency, coupling and complexity.

sections.title: What patterns are and where to find them
sections.summary: Defines architectural vs design patterns and surveys the main catalogues of cloud patterns an architect can borrow from.

notes.lead: A named, reusable solution to a recurring problem in a context.
items: **Architectural patterns** → **high-level ideas** aimed at qualities like **performance limits**, **availability** and **business risk**
**Design patterns** → the more **local, formalised best-practice templates**
**Benefit** → **lowers risk** and gives the team a **shared vocabulary**

notes.h: Cloud patterns evolved with the platform
items: **VM era** → **IaaS stack**
**Container era** → **Kubernetes control plane and nodes**

notes.lead: Several catalogues cover the same ground with different groupings.
items: **Richardson's microservices.io** → organises by **application**, **application-infrastructure** and **infrastructure** patterns
**Erl's** → by concern: **scaling, reliability, data, security, monitoring**
**Pick the catalogue** that matches your **problem category**
**Quote the pattern's problem, mechanism and trade-offs** when **justifying a design**

terms.def: Reusable description of a high-level design idea addressing qualities like availability and performance.
General reusable solution to a commonly occurring problem in a given design context.
Give clients a restricted, time-limited token to access a resource (e.g. storage) directly.
Gradually replace a legacy system by routing features one at a time to new services.

check.q: In a design review, a teammate proposes a home-grown mechanism for letting clients upload files directly to storage with temporary access. You recognise it as a known pattern. Why does naming it matter?

items: **Naming it** gives the team a **shared vocabulary**
Brings the pattern's known **problem**, **mechanism** and **trade-offs**, such as limiting the **scope and lifetime of the key**
→ the design is easier to **justify** and **review**
a.foot: A **home-grown** version risks rediscovering those trade-offs **in production**.

check.q: A team's problem is cascading failures between services. Which group of a cloud pattern catalogue would you search first, and what would you expect to find?

items: **Expect**: **Circuit Breaker**, **Retry**, **Bulkhead**, **Health Endpoint Monitoring** → address **failing dependencies**
**Catalogues group the same patterns differently** → pick the one whose grouping matches the **problem category**
**Compare the candidates' trade-offs** instead of applying the first match

sections.title: Container and microservice patterns
sections.summary: How cloud native layers good code, DDD, microservices and Kubernetes, plus container patterns (sidecar, adapter, ambassador, chain) and microservice/event-driven pattern families.

items: **Clean code**
inside **domain-driven design**
inside **microservice principles** → **optimised for change**
inside **Kubernetes patterns** → **automatable containers at scale**
notes.foot: Allowing a **polyglot world** where each service **chooses its own language and database**.

items: **Single-concern**
**Disposable**
**Immutable**
**Self-contained**
**Small Linux process**
**API-driven**
**Observable**
notes.foot: **Immutability and disposability** make **scaling, rolling updates and self-healing** safe.

items: **Sidecar** → helper container **in the same pod** adds **cross-cutting features** (**logging, proxying, config**) **without touching app code**
**Adapter** → **normalises the app's output** (e.g. **monitoring format**)
**Ambassador** → **proxies outbound connections** (e.g. to the **right DB per environment**)
**Container chain** → fixes the **start/stop order** of sidecars and main app
**Decomposition**
**Database per service**
**Gateway/aggregation**
**Sync chains** vs **async pub/sub messaging**
**Shared data** → an **early decoupling stage**
**Event sourcing** and **CQRS**
**Erl's API/proxy/versioning** patterns
**Coordinate through events** on a **broker** (e.g. **Kafka**)
**One service publishes**, the **next reacts**
**Event store** feeds **databases and analytics**

terms.def: Helper container alongside the main container in a pod adding cross-cutting features.
Sidecar that proxies the app's outbound connections to external services.
Sidecar that converts the app's output into a standard format.
Defined start/stop order for a pod's sidecar and main containers.

check.q: Twelve services in four languages must all ship logs in one format and route database connections per environment. Would you build this into each app, or use container patterns?

items: **Adapter sidecar**: converts each app's **log output** to the **standard format**
**Ambassador sidecar**: **proxies outbound database connections** to the right target **for each environment**
Both work in **any language** without changing **app code**
a.foot: Cost: **extra containers per pod** and a defined **start and stop order** (a **container chain**).

check.q: A team patches running containers in place to fix a bug, and the next autoscaling event brings back the bug. Which container properties were ignored?

items: New instances start from the **unchanged image** → **in-place fixes are lost** and instances **drift apart**
**Fix**: build a **new image** with the fix and **roll it out**
→ any instance can be **killed and replaced** by an identical one

check.q: An order service must notify billing, shipping and analytics, and each team keeps asking the order team to add a new call. Which microservice pattern family helps?

items: The order service **publishes events** to a **broker**; each **consumer reacts on its own**
**New consumers subscribe** without changing the order service
An **event store** can also feed **databases** and **analytics**
a.foot: Cost: **eventual consistency**, and the need for **central logging and tracing** to follow a flow.

items.label: Sidecar
items.detail: Enhances and extends the main container in the same pod: platform abstraction, proxy to remote services, logging, configuration.

items.label: Adapter
items.detail: Simplifies the app container's complex monitoring output for the monitoring service.

items.label: Ambassador
items.detail: Proxies the app's database connections (e.g. to production, test or local databases).

items.label: Container chain
items.detail: Defined order of starting and stopping the sidecar containers around the main container.

sections.title: Event sourcing, service mesh and circuit breaker
sections.summary: Event sourcing (state as events) with its pros and cons, then service mesh and circuit breaker as ways to make inter-service calls reliable.

items: **Append** an **OrderCreated** or **OrderApproved** event **atomically**
**Reconstruct state by replay**
**Lecture**: the **event store** also exposes **durable subscriptions** → avoids a separate **state-write and message-publish** operation
**Separate external broker** → still needs **reliable delivery integration**
notes.foot: Event sourcing alone does **not** make **unrelated systems commit atomically**.

items: **Event append** → can be **atomic**
**Projections and subscribers** → **catch up asynchronously**
**Audit history and replay** → help **recovery** and **analytics**
**Complexity** → **evolving events**, **rebuilding views**, **growing storage**

notes.lead: Moves inter-service plumbing out of the app.
items: **Requests flow through proxies**
**Dedicated infrastructure layer**
**Proxies run alongside each service** as **sidecars**
**Together** → form a **mesh network**
**Problem** → when a **synchronous callee** is **down or slow**, callers **hold threads**, **exhaust resources** and **fail too**
**Proxy counts successes and failures**
**Past an error-rate threshold** → **trips** so calls **fail immediately**
**API gateway** should **protect itself** this way

terms.def: Persist an entity as an append-only sequence of state-changing events; replay to get current state.
Database of events with APIs to append, read and subscribe.
Saved current state so only later events need replaying.
Infrastructure layer of sidecar proxies managing service-to-service traffic.
Proxy that stops calling a failing service once its error rate passes a threshold.

check.q: A service saves an order to its database and then publishes 'OrderCreated' to a broker. Sometimes the save succeeds but the publish fails. How does the lecture's event-sourcing design avoid this, and what doesn't it solve?

items: **The event append is the state change**: **OrderCreated** is written **atomically** to the **event store**
**Subscribers** read that **committed history** → no separate **save-then-publish** step to fall out of sync
**Doesn't solve**: an **external broker** or a **remote subscriber** isn't part of the same commit → integrating with them still needs **reliable delivery**

check.q: A team wants event sourcing for a simple product-catalogue service 'for the audit trail'. What would you weigh?

items: **Benefits**: **full history** for **audit**; **replay** for **recovery** and **analytics**

sub: **Querying current state** is hard, often needing **CQRS read models**
**Storage grows** because all history is kept

a.foot: For a **simple catalogue**, an **audit log table** may give enough history at a fraction of the complexity.

check.q: When a recommendation service slows down, the product service's threads all wait on it, and the product pages fail too. Give the cause, a countermeasure and its drawback.

items: **Cause**: **synchronous calls** to a **slow callee** hold **threads** until **resources are exhausted** → the failure **cascades**
**Countermeasure**: a **circuit breaker** counts failures and, past an **error-rate threshold**, **trips** → calls **fail immediately**
**Fallback**: such as showing the page **without recommendations**
**Drawback**: while the breaker is **open**, even requests that **might have succeeded are rejected** → **thresholds** and **recovery probes** need tuning

sections.title: Data store, CQRS and saga patterns
sections.summary: Database-per-service vs shared database, then CQRS for cross-service queries and saga (choreography vs orchestration) for cross-service transactions.

notes.h: Database per service vs shared database
items: **Per service** → data **private behind an API** → **loose coupling** and **independent evolution**
**Per service cost** → **cross-service queries and transactions** get hard
**Shared DB** → **local ACID** and **easy joins**, but **couples services**
**If you share** → do it **within a domain boundary only**
**Lecture example** → builds an **Order History view** from **events published by owning services**
**Materialised view** → makes **cross-service reads efficient**
**Cost** → can **lag behind writes**
**Not required** in every implementation → **event sourcing** or **physically separate databases**
**Atomic operations**
**History for analytics**
**Separate scalable read and write models**
**Slim read DTOs**
**Cost** → **extra infrastructure**, and **complexity** if models are **poorly designed**
**Saga** → a **sequence of local transactions** with **compensating transactions** on failure
**Choreography** → services **react to each other's events** (e.g. **Order Created**, then **Credit Reserved** or **Credit Limit Exceeded**), **no controller**
**Orchestration** → a **central orchestrator** sending **commands** (**Reserve Credit**)
**Choreography suits** → **simple flows**
**Orchestration suits** → **many steps** or **branching**
notes.foot: A saga is **not one isolated ACID transaction**: **intermediate results can be visible**, and **compensation is a new business operation**.

terms.def: Each service owns a private datastore accessed only via its API.
Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate write and read models; distinct stores and event-fed views are implementation options.
Sequence of local transactions across services, with compensating actions on failure.
Saga coordination by services reacting to each other's events, no central controller.
Saga coordination where a central orchestrator sends commands to participants.

check.q: Order and Customer services each own their database, and a support screen needs 'all orders with customer names'. Joining across the databases is not allowed. What are the options?

items: **API composition**: a **composer** calls both services and **joins the results in memory** → simple but **slow for large results**
**CQRS**: build a **read-optimised view** from both services' **events** → fast but **lags behind writes**
**Sharing tables**: would make the join easy but **couples the services' releases**

check.q: An order flow has 7 steps with branching for credit checks, stock and fraud review. Choreography or orchestration for the saga?

items: **Many steps and branches** → a **central orchestrator** keeps the flow in one place where it can be **followed**, **monitored** and **changed**
**Choreography** suits **simple flows** with **few participants**: each service **reacting to events** avoids a coordinator but **scatters the logic**
a.foot: The orchestrator must itself be **durable** and must **not take over the services' business logic**.

check.q: A saga charges a card, then stock reservation fails, so the saga issues a refund. A teammate calls this 'a rollback'. Why is that misleading?

items: **The charge was committed**: may already have been seen by the **customer** or the **bank**
**A refund is a new business action** with its own outcome and **possible failure**, not an **erasure of history**
**Intermediate states are visible**: a saga isn't one isolated **ACID transaction**
**Design**: **persist saga progress**; make each step and **compensation** **safe to retry**

check.q: A team uses CQRS without event sourcing, updating the read view from the write database's changes. Is that valid?

items: **CQRS** only separates the **command** and **query models**; it doesn't require **event sourcing** or **separate physical databases** in every implementation
**Event sourcing pairs well** with CQRS: the event store is **poor at queries** and **supplies events to project**
**Without it**: the team must still handle **view lag** and **rebuilding the view**

visuals.title: Saga: choreography vs orchestration
rows: Each local transaction publishes domain events that trigger local transactions in other services
An orchestrator (object) tells the participants what local transactions to execute
Order Created event, then Credit Reserved or Credit Limit Exceeded
Create Order Saga sends a Reserve Credit command via the message broker; reply is Reserve Credit Response

sections.title: Sharding strategies
sections.summary: Why one data server is not enough and the three ways to split data across shards.

notes.lead: A single data server runs into limits:
items: **Storage**
**Compute** under **concurrent queries**
**Network bandwidth**
**Geography** → **legal, compliance or latency** reasons to keep data **near users**
**Lookup** → a **map routes by shard key** (e.g. **tenant ID**); tenants can be **placed or moved** → good for **multi-tenancy** and **residency**
**Range** → **sequential keys** keep **related data together** (**orders by month**) → good for **range queries** but prone to **hotspots**
**Hash** → a **hash of the key** spreads **distinct keys**, can **reduce hotspots** → but **range queries touch many shards**
**One very hot key** can still **dominate a hash shard**

terms.def: Attribute deciding which shard a record lives in.
A shard receiving a disproportionate share of load.

check.q: An orders table is sharded by order month, and every December the current shard is overloaded while the others sit idle. Diagnose this and propose a change.

items: **Diagnosis**: **range sharding** on a **sequential key** puts all current writes on the **newest shard** → a **hotspot**
**Change**: **hash sharding** by **order or customer ID** → spreads writes across shards
**Cost**: queries by **date range** now **fan out** to every shard
**Mitigation**: keep a separate **date-indexed read view** if **month reports** are frequent

check.q: A multi-tenant SaaS has a few very large tenants and must keep EU tenants' data in the EU. Which sharding strategy fits, and why?

a.lead: **Lookup sharding** with **tenant ID** as the **shard key**.
items: The **map** can place each tenant on a **specific shard**
**Residency**: in the right **region**
**Large tenant** → move onto a **dedicated shard**
a.foot: Cost: the **lookup map** becomes a **critical component**, and **tenant moves** need careful **migration**.

check.q: After hash sharding, one shard is still overloaded. Records are evenly spread. What is the likely cause?

items: One very busy **tenant or item** sends most of the **traffic** to its shard
**Hashing spreads distinct keys**, not the traffic on a single key
**Fix**: **balance by actual traffic**, for example by moving that tenant to **its own shard** with a **lookup**, or adding **caching** for it

items.label: Lookup
items.detail: A map routes a request to the shard containing the data using the shard key, e.g. tenant ID in a multi-tenant app.

items.label: Range
items.detail: Groups related items in the same shard, ordered by sequential shard keys.

items.label: Hash
items.detail: Hashing spreads distinct keys across shards, reducing skew from ordered keys. It cannot divide the work for one hot key by itself.

sections.title: Multi-tenancy models
sections.summary: The isolate-vs-share continuum for architecture, schema, storage and deployment, plus SaaS managed-service capabilities and maturity levels.

notes.lead: Shares application or infrastructure resources among tenants while keeping their data and access logically separated.
items: **One codebase** serves **many customers** with **tenant-specific configuration**
**Isolation and sharing vary by layer**

sub: but **few tenants per server** and **cost rises fast**
use when tenants **need isolation and will pay**

items: **Separated schema** → **one DB**, a **schema per tenant**

sub: use when **co-mingling is acceptable** and **custom fields are predictable**

items: **Structured vs unstructured**
**Query needs** → **key/value** is **weak for complex queries**
**Aggregation**
**Scale-out**
**Transactions**
**Backup/DR**
**Security/audit**

terms.def: Multiple customer groups share a service or infrastructure with deliberate tenant isolation and potentially different configurations.
One database with a separate schema per tenant.
All tenants share tables, distinguished by a tenant ID column.
Using different data store types for different needs in one system.

check.q: A bank-grade client of a SaaS product demands strict isolation and will pay extra. Which schema option, and why not the cheaper ones?

items: **Strongest isolation**, **security** and room for **customisation**
**Higher cost** and **fewer tenants per server** → covered by the **premium**
**Separated schema**: shares a **database engine**
**Shared schema**: **co-mingles rows** by **TenantID**
a.foot: The cheaper options may **not meet the client's isolation demand**.

check.q: A SaaS for small shops has 20,000 tenants, mostly on the same plan, and a few need extra fields. Which schema option fits, and what problem should you expect?

items: **Maximises tenants per server**
**Predefined custom fields** fit if the extra fields are **predictable**
**Problem**: reserved **generic custom columns** that most tenants leave empty → **sparse tables**
**Co-mingled data** → every query must **filter by tenant** → strict **access control** and **testing**

check.q: A SaaS provider wants enterprise tenants on isolated infrastructure and small tenants sharing everything, all from one codebase. Is that a contradiction?

a.lead: **No.** Multi-tenancy is a **continuum** applied **at each layer**.
items: **Layers**: **deployment** (**bare-metal or VM** versus **shared containers**), **runtime**, **application**, **storage**
**One codebase** with **tenant-specific configuration** can serve **shared** and **isolated tiers**
**Toward isolation**: more **security**, **control** and **customisation** at **higher cost**
**Toward sharing**: **economies of scale**

visuals.title: Multi-tenant schema options (slide 47)
rows: Separate database per tenant; database maintains data dictionary
One shared database, a separate schema (set of tables) per tenant
All tenants' data in one database; pre-defined custom fields
Few tenants per database server; infrastructure cost rises quickly

sections.title: Content aggregation patterns
sections.summary: Four places to combine data from many microservices for one screen: client, API gateway, composite microservice, or database.

notes.h: Where to assemble one screen's data
notes.lead: One screen's data from many services:
items: **Client**
**API gateway**
**Composite microservice**
**Database**
notes.foot: Each **moves the logic further from the UI** and **adds cost**.

items: **Client-side calls** → can **render parts of a screen as each result arrives**, but **expose coordination to the client**
**Gateway aggregation** → **reduces external round trips** and **hides internals**
**Complete combined response** → may **wait for its slowest required backend**
**Mitigation** → **deliberate timeouts** or **partial results** where the experience allows them
**Composite service** applies **real-time business logic** during aggregation
**Pros** → **finer control**, **less gateway dependence**
**Cost** → **extra hop**, **more code**, **more failure points**, **reactive/callback code** for **parallel calls**
**Pre-aggregate** into an **operational data store** (often a **document DB**)
**Most flexible, analytics-enriched views** → such as **customer 360**
**Cost** → **complexity**, **duplicated data**, **ETL** or **change data capture**

terms.def: DDD boundary within which one model and its service/DB apply.
Central store of pre-aggregated operational data, often a document DB.
Capturing changes from a source database to propagate elsewhere.

check.q: A mobile app on slow networks needs a dashboard built from 5 services. Client or gateway aggregation?

items: **One request instead of five** → suits **limited bandwidth** and **weak devices**
**Hides the internal services**
**Risk**: the combined response **waits for the slowest required service** → set **timeouts** and return **partial results** where the screen allows
a.foot: **Client aggregation** would let parts **render as they arrive**, but costs **five round trips** on a slow network.

check.q: While a dashboard is aggregated, a discount must be calculated from loyalty tier and basket contents. Should that logic live in the gateway?

a.lead: **No.** It belongs in a **composite microservice** in the **business tier**.
items: **Real-time business logic** during aggregation goes there, not in the gateway
The **gateway** stays focused on **routing** and **cross-cutting concerns**
**Cost**: an **extra hop**, more **code**, more **failure points**; **parallel calls** need **reactive or callback** code

check.q: A customer-360 view needs orders, support tickets and churn scores from analytics, and must load in under a second. Which aggregation pattern fits, and what does it cost?

items: **Pre-aggregate** into an **operational data store**, often a **document database**
→ the view loads with **one read** and can include **analytics**
**Cost**: **duplicated data**, **extra storage**, **ETL** or **change-data-capture** pipelines
**Freshness**: only as fresh as the **last sync**

visuals.title: Where to aggregate service data
rows: Needs sophisticated UI (Ajax / SPA); aggregation knowledge exposed at the UI
May wait for slow required backends; choose timeout and partial-result policy
Extra hop and more code; parallel aggregation needs reactive or callback code
More complexity; data duplication and extra storage; ETL or CDC tools needed

sections.title: Microservice coordination and design checklist
sections.summary: Capabilities needed to coordinate multi-service flows and the closing cloud-native design checklist and summary map.

items: **State management** → outputs kept in a **persistent store** safe from failure
**Transaction control**
**Post-call coordination** → collect each call's **success or failure** and **decide the next step**
**Timeout handling** → a **per-microflow timer** raising an event on the **event bus**
**Configurability** of **timers and compensations**
**2PC** → coordinates an **atomic distributed commit**, but can **hold locks** and **block during failures**; participants must **support the protocol**
**Saga** → **local commits** and **business compensations**, **reducing synchronous coordination**, at the cost of **intermediate states** and **recovery logic**
**App design** and **tenancy model**
**Scale** and **zero-downtime upgrades**
**Data store** → **redundancy, partitioning, caching**
**Security** → **encryption, token auth, auditing, SSO**
**Integration formats** and **per-tenant SLAs**
**Middleware** → **config, queues, discovery, monitoring**
**Economics** → **cost and revenue models**
**Service Architecture** → **multi-tenancy**, **capacity**, **data/service/security patterns**
**Operational Structure** → **monitoring, billing, deployment, SLA, compliance, risk**

terms.def: New business action that semantically reverses or offsets an earlier committed step; it can also fail and need recovery.
Distributed transaction protocol where all participants prepare then commit together.
Short coordinated flow of service calls managed by a composite service.

check.q: A payment call from a composite service times out. A developer retries by creating a new payment. What could go wrong, and what is the safe approach?

items: **Risk**: the **timeout doesn't prove the payment failed**; the provider may have **charged** before the response was lost → a new payment can **charge twice**
**Safe approach**: reuse a **stable operation identifier**; **query or reconcile** the original result before **retrying or compensating**
**Coordination layer**: keeps that state in a **persistent store** safe from failure

check.q: Two services in different teams must both commit or both abort a transfer. One proposes 2PC, the other a saga. What decides it?

a.lead: **The invariant and the participants** decide it.
items: **2PC**: **atomic distributed commit**, but **holds locks**, can **block** when a participant fails, and every participant must **support the protocol**
**Saga**: **local commits** with **business compensations** → reduces **synchronous coupling**, but **exposes intermediate states**
a.foot: If **brief intermediate states** are acceptable to the business, a **saga** usually fits **independent services** better.

check.q: A composite flow calls 4 services, and one never responds. The flow hangs forever. Which coordination capabilities are missing?

items: **Timeout handling**: a **timer for each flow** that **raises an event** when it expires
**Post-call coordination**: collecting each call's **success or failure** and deciding the **next step**
**State management**: progress **survives a crash**
**Configurable** timers and compensations: different steps need **different limits**

exam_angles.q: Design order processing on microservices where placing an order must reserve customer credit in a separate Customer service. A teammate proposes a shared database to keep it simple. Evaluate that, then design the consistency mechanism and say what users may see.

sub: But **couples** the two services' **schemas and releases** → keep **data private**

items: **Choreograph** it through **events** for this **two-step flow**, or **orchestrate** if steps will grow
**Reliability**: **persist progress**, use **stable command identifiers** and **timeouts**; **compensate** (**cancel the order**) if credit fails
a.foot: **What users may see**: a brief **'pending'** order, because a saga **exposes intermediate states**.

exam_angles.q: A SaaS provider serves 5,000 small businesses and 4 regulated enterprise clients, two of which require in-country data. Propose a multi-tenancy, schema and sharding strategy, and state the trade-offs.

items: **Small tenants**: **shared schema** (**TenantID** with **predefined custom fields**) → **economies of scale**
**Regulated tenants**: **separated database**, or **VM-level isolation**, charged as a **premium tier**
**Lookup sharding** by **tenant ID**: places each tenant, including the **in-country** ones in **local regions**, and can move a **large tenant** to its own shard

sub: Shared side: possibly **sparse shared tables** and **strict tenant filtering**
Isolated side: **higher infrastructure and operating cost**

exam_angles.q: An order-history page must show data from Order, Kitchen, Delivery and Accounting services within 300 ms. API composition is too slow. Design the read side, and decide whether event sourcing is needed.

a.lead: A **CQRS read model**; **event sourcing is optional**.
items: **Order History view** updated from the **four services' domain events** → the page reads **one pre-joined store**
**View lag**: a **just-placed order** may briefly be missing
Handle **duplicate** and **out-of-order events** and **rebuilding the view**
**Event sourcing**: adopt only if **authoritative event history** for **audit and recovery** justifies the **modelling and infrastructure cost**
Otherwise **publish events** from each service's **normal writes**

exam_angles.q: A slow downstream service took down an entire platform last month: gateway threads were exhausted and every API failed. Explain the failure, then design protection at the gateway and between services, naming one drawback.

items: **Failure**: **synchronous calls** to a **slow callee** held **threads** until the **gateway ran out** → one dependency's slowness became **everyone's outage**
**Timeouts** on every call
**Circuit breaker** at the **gateway** and in **callers**: trips past an **error-rate threshold** → calls **fail fast**, with **fallbacks** or **partial responses**
Apply it consistently through **sidecars** or a **service mesh** rather than per-app code
a.foot: **Drawback**: an **open breaker** rejects some requests that would have succeeded, and **badly tuned thresholds** can trip too often.

exam_angles.q: A customer portal home page combines profile, orders, recommendations, support tickets and a churn score. Users are on mobile and desktop. Compare the four aggregation patterns for this page and recommend a combination.

a.lead: **Recommend gateway aggregation** for mobile, with **timeouts** and **partial results**, and **pre-aggregate** the **churn score** and **ticket summary** in the data store.

sub: **Renders parts as they arrive** on desktop
Costs **round trips** on mobile and **exposes coordination in the UI**
Can apply **business logic**, such as **ranking recommendations**

exam_angles.q: A global app's data store has hit single-server limits on write throughput, and EU users' data must stay in the EU. Recommend a sharding approach and name two operational side effects to plan for.

items: **First confirm the limit**: **write compute**, **storage**, **bandwidth** or **geography**
**Lookup sharding** by **region or tenant** → **EU residency**
**Within a region**: **hash by customer ID** → spreads writes and avoids the **hotspots** that **range sharding on dates** would create

sub: **Cross-shard queries and reports** get slower and more complex
**Rebalancing** when shards fill or a **hot key** appears needs **data migration**

a.foot: **Balance by actual traffic**, not record counts.
